# Get started on the Raspberry Pi Pico W

<!-- type: how-to · level: 1 -->

**Needs first:** [Install](../start/install.md)

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED by scripts/gen-board-support.py: starter status -->
> **Status:** Boots, manual (2026-11-01); reads *Builds* from 2027-03-02. From the board support registry: [`nros-board-rpi-pico-w-zephyr`](../reference/boards/rpi-pico-w-zephyr.md); [Board Support Levels](../reference/board-support-levels.md) explains the words. The image runs in the board's twin, `wokwi:pi-pico-w`, and on the board, `rpi-pico-w`. Each run in this twin needs your own `WOKWI_CLI_TOKEN`, so nano-ros CI never runs it.
<!-- END GENERATED starter status -->

This starter puts a C talker on a Raspberry Pi Pico W (RP2040, Cortex-M0+)
running Zephyr 3.7, talking to ROS 2 over a serial link. You do not need the
board to start: [Wokwi](https://wokwi.com) simulates it, and its serial
monitor carries UART0, the board's zenoh link, to your host. The image you run
in Wokwi is the image you later flash to the board.

Wokwi is a hosted simulator. The simulation runs on Wokwi's servers, not on
your machine, so every run in the twin needs network access and a Wokwi token
of your own, and spends your Wokwi account's simulation minutes (a run takes
about a minute and a half). nano-ros CI never runs this twin: you run it, with
your token.

## What you need

- A Linux host with the [install](../start/install.md) done, so `nros` is on
  your `PATH`, and ROS 2 Humble with `ros-humble-rmw-zenoh-cpp`.
- A Wokwi account and a CI token for it, from your
  [Wokwi dashboard](https://wokwi.com/dashboard/ci). Put it in the shell you
  run the twin from, and keep it out of any file you commit:

  ```text
  export WOKWI_CLI_TOKEN=<your token>
  ```

- For the last step only: a Pico W, a USB cable, and a 3.3 V USB-to-UART
  adapter for UART0 (GP0 and GP1), the board's zenoh link. Everything before
  it runs in the twin.
- Zephyr's host tools: `west` and the build tools
  [Zephyr's Getting Started](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/3.7.0/develop/getting_started/index.html)
  lists, plus `socat`, which joins Wokwi's serial monitor to a terminal device
  on your host. `nros setup` installs no system packages, so install them
  yourself. On Debian or Ubuntu:

```bash probe=30 track=installed
sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends git cmake ninja-build gperf \
    device-tree-compiler python3-pip python3-venv xz-utils file wget socat
pip3 install --user west
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
```

The serial link is the only one this board has here. WiFi is deferred: Zephyr
3.7 has no driver for the Pico W's CYW43439 radio on its SPI bus, and the
driver arrives with the Zephyr 4.4 line.

## Provision

Provision the board:

```bash probe=32 track=installed
nros setup rpi-pico-w-zephyr --rmw zenoh
export ZEPHYR_SDK_INSTALL_DIR="$(nros locate tool zephyr-sdk)"
```

That fetches what the board needs into a shared store under `~/.nros`: the
Zephyr SDK, the zenoh-pico sources, the Rust target, and `wokwi-cli`, the
client that drives the twin. It installs no router: the router is ROS's
`rmw_zenohd`, from your ROS 2 install.

Zephyr's sources live in a west workspace of your own. This one pins Zephyr
3.7 and fetches only the modules the board builds with, `hal_rpi_pico` among
them (`import: true` would fetch every vendor's HAL):

```bash probe=34 track=installed
mkdir -p pico_ws/manifest && cd pico_ws
cat > manifest/west.yml <<'WEST_YML'
manifest:
  remotes:
    - name: zephyrproject-rtos
      url-base: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos
  projects:
    - name: zephyr
      remote: zephyrproject-rtos
      revision: v3.7.0
      import:
        name-allowlist: [cmsis, picolibc, mbedtls, tinycrypt, mcuboot, net-tools, hal_rpi_pico]
    # Zephyr's Rust support. The board's setup patches it, so the workspace
    # needs it even for a C talker. Pinned to the revision nano-ros builds
    # with on the 3.7 line (it has no release tags).
    - name: zephyr-lang-rust
      remote: zephyrproject-rtos
      revision: 404fcefdbab0f2711cd342a1fab9d2eda52a1ba9
      path: modules/lang/rust
  self:
    path: manifest
WEST_YML
west init -l manifest
west update --narrow -o=--depth=1
pip3 install --user -r zephyr/scripts/requirements-base.txt
export ZEPHYR_BASE="$PWD/zephyr"
```

Last, give the west workspace the patches nano-ros carries for Zephyr 3.7:

```bash probe=36 track=installed
nros setup board rpi-pico-w-zephyr --zephyr-workspace "$PWD"
```

## Scaffold the project

```bash probe=40 track=installed
nros new pico_ws --board rpi-pico-w-zephyr --template talker --lang c
cd pico_ws
```

That wrote a workspace with two packages: `src/pico_node/`, the C talker, and
`src/pico_node_bringup/`, which says what the talker runs on. The board
reaches the router on your host through UART0, which Zephyr calls
`uart@40034000`, at 115200 baud. Say so with one line at the end of the
bringup's `system.toml`:

```bash probe=45 track=installed
echo 'locator = "serial/uart@40034000#baudrate=115200"' >> src/pico_node_bringup/system.toml
```

The line lands in the `[image.zephyr]` block, under the
`board = "rpi-pico-w-zephyr"` line the scaffold wrote. The board's own
configuration gives UART0 to zenoh and puts the console on UART1 (GP4 and
GP5). It also sizes nano-ros to fit the RP2040's 264 KiB of RAM, so a talker
needs no settings of its own.

## Run it in the Wokwi twin

Source ROS 2, check that your token is set, then build and run. ROS 2 provides
the router, and its message definitions are what the build generates the
talker's `std_msgs` code from. This first run records the ROS 2 prefix in the
workspace, so later runs of it need no sourced shell:

```bash probe=50 probe-run=1500 track=installed
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
test -n "$WOKWI_CLI_TOKEN"
nros run pico_node --expect 'Publishing:'
```

```text probe-expect=50
Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
nros run: matched after
```

`nros run` builds the firmware through west (the first build takes a few
minutes; later ones take seconds), starts the board in Wokwi with UART0 on a
terminal device of your host, starts `rmw_zenohd` on that device, and prints
the board's console. With `--expect` it stops everything and exits 0 at the
first console line containing that text, and exits 1 if the board stops
first.

Without `--expect` it keeps running until you press Ctrl-C, or until Wokwi
ends the session (the free plan's sessions last five minutes). Start it that
way in one terminal:

```bash probe=60 probe-run=300 probe-keep track=installed
nros run pico_node
```

```text probe-expect=60
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
```

## Flash the board

On the bench, wire the USB-to-UART adapter to GP0 (TX) and GP1 (RX) and
ground, plug both the Pico W and the adapter into your host, and flash the
same image:

```bash
nros flash --monitor
```

> **Not replayed.** No probe runs this flash line (a CI runner has no board), so it is written from the board's runner, not measured ([tracking issue](https://github.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/blob/main/docs/issues/archived/2176-unprobed-fvp-sitl-flash-lines.md)).

`nros flash` builds the image if it is stale and programs it through
Zephyr's own runner for the board: hold BOOTSEL while you plug the Pico W in,
and the image is copied onto the drive it shows. With `--monitor` it then
serves the board's link on your host: UART0 arrives through the adapter as a
USB serial device (`/dev/ttyUSB0`, say), and the router listens there. Name
the device with `--port` when more than one is attached. The console, UART1,
needs a second adapter if you want to read it.

## See it in ROS 2

With the talker running, in the twin or on the board, ask ROS 2 for the topic
from a second terminal. The router `nros run` started also listens where a
ROS 2 node on this machine looks for one, so nothing needs to be configured:

```bash probe=70 probe-run=120 track=installed
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort
```

```text probe-expect=70
data: 'Hello World:
```

The talker publishes best-effort, so the echo asks for best-effort too.
Ctrl-C in the first terminal ends the Wokwi session and stops the router.

## If it doesn't work

- **The `test -n "$WOKWI_CLI_TOKEN"` line fails, or `wokwi-cli` says
  `Missing WOKWI_CLI_TOKEN`:** this shell has no token. Export it, as under
  [What you need](#what-you-need).
- **`nros run` says no runner package drives `wokwi` yet:** this release of
  `nros` cannot start the Wokwi twin itself. The steps up to the build still
  hold, and [Flash the board](#flash-the-board) runs the same image on a
  Pico W.
- **Wokwi refuses the session for quota:** your account's simulation minutes
  are spent. They come back over a rolling 30 days, or with a paid plan.
- **A build that cannot find `hal_rpi_pico`:** the west workspace predates the
  `hal_rpi_pico` line in its allowlist. Add it and run `west update` again.
- **Everything else:** [Troubleshooting - First 10 Minutes](../reference/troubleshooting-index.md).
